questions.title: IAM Roles, Policies and Least Privilege
questions.question: How does AWS IAM work and how do you implement least privilege for a Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- IAM: Identity and Access Management — controls who can do what on AWS resources
- User: human identity with long-term credentials (avoid for applications)
- Role: temporary credentials — assumed by EC2, ECS tasks, Lambda; no long-term keys
- Policy: JSON document defining allowed/denied actions on resources
- Least privilege: grant only what the application actually needs
- Trust policy: defines who (principal) can assume the role
- Never hardcode AWS access keys in code — always use IAM roles

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
IAM controls access to AWS resources. The key concepts are users for human identities, roles for service identities, and policies that define what actions are allowed or denied on which resources.

For a Java application, never use IAM users with access keys. Create an IAM role and attach it to your EC2 instance, ECS task, or Lambda. The AWS SDK automatically retrieves temporary credentials from the instance metadata service. These credentials rotate automatically every few hours — far more secure than static keys.

Least privilege means granting the minimum permissions necessary. If your application only reads from DynamoDB, don't give it dynamodb:* — give it specifically dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:Query on the exact table ARNs it needs. This limits the blast radius if the application is ever compromised.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: IAM controls access to AWS resources.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This limits the blast radius if the application is ever compromised.

questions.title: Cross-Account Access and Role Assumption
questions.question: How does cross-account role assumption work in AWS and when would a Java application need it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Cross-account: application in Account A assumes a role in Account B
- STS AssumeRole: returns temporary credentials for the target role
- Trust relationship: target role must explicitly trust the source account/role
- External ID: extra verification — prevents confused deputy attack from third parties
- Session duration: 15 min to 12 hours; SDK refreshes automatically
- Java SDK: StsAssumeRoleCredentialsProvider for transparent credential management

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Cross-account role assumption is how an application in one AWS account accesses resources in another. Your application calls STS AssumeRole, provides the ARN of a role in the other account, and receives temporary credentials. You then use those credentials to access the target account's resources.

This is common in organizations that separate environments into different accounts — prod, staging, dev — or have a shared services account for centralized logging or artifact storage.

The trust relationship on the target role is the security gate. It explicitly defines which accounts or specific roles can assume it. The target account's owner fully controls who gets access.

questions.title: AWS Cognito with Spring Security
questions.question: How do you integrate AWS Cognito for authentication in a Spring Boot REST API?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Cognito User Pool: managed user directory — sign up, login, MFA, password policies
- Cognito issues JWT access tokens (RS256 signed) after authentication
- Spring Security validates JWT against Cognito's JWKS endpoint (public keys)
- Resource Server: no network call per request — local cryptographic validation
- JWT claims: sub (user ID), email, cognito:groups
- Groups → Spring Security roles mapping via JwtAuthenticationConverter

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
AWS Cognito User Pool manages user registration, sign-in, and token issuance. After authentication, the user receives a JWT access token signed by Cognito's private key.

Your Spring Boot API validates these tokens as an OAuth2 Resource Server. Spring fetches Cognito's public keys from the JWKS endpoint at startup and validates each incoming JWT cryptographically — no network call to Cognito per request. If the signature is valid and the token hasn't expired, the request is authenticated.

Cognito groups map to Spring Security roles. You configure a JwtAuthenticationConverter to read the cognito:groups claim and convert group names to GrantedAuthority, enabling @PreAuthorize and hasRole checks throughout the application.

speakable_v2.hook: AWS Cognito User Pool manages user registration, sign-in, and token issuance.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: You configure a JwtAuthenticationConverter to read the cognito:groups claim and convert group names to GrantedAuthority, enabling @PreAuthorize and hasRole checks throughout the application.

questions.title: IAM Permission Boundaries and SCPs
questions.question: What are IAM permission boundaries and Service Control Policies, and when do you use each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Permission boundary: cap on maximum permissions a role can have — prevents privilege escalation
- Even if identity policy allows s3:* but boundary only allows s3:GetObject → only GetObject works
- Effective permissions: intersection of identity policy AND permission boundary
- SCP (Service Control Policy): org-level guardrails applied to entire accounts or OUs
- SCP + IAM policy: both must allow — SCP is a ceiling on what any identity can do in that account
- Use case: allow developer teams to create their own roles, but cap what those roles can do
- Deny: explicit deny in any policy always overrides allow

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Permission boundaries are a maximum permissions cap. Even if a role's policy grants broad access, the permission boundary limits what it can actually do. The effective permissions are the intersection of what the identity policy allows and what the boundary allows. This is useful for delegating role creation to developers while preventing them from creating overly powerful roles — you set a boundary that caps what any role they create can do.

Service Control Policies operate at the AWS Organizations level and apply to entire accounts or organizational units. An SCP is a ceiling on what any identity in that account can do, regardless of how permissive their IAM policies are. If an SCP denies ec2:* for a dev account, no one in that account can create EC2 instances — not even the root user.

The rule is: effective permissions = what identity policy allows AND what SCP allows AND what permission boundary allows. An explicit deny anywhere overrides everything. This layered model lets organizations enforce security guardrails at the org level while delegating day-to-day access management to individual teams.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Permission boundaries are a maximum permissions cap.
speakable_v2.cap: This layered model lets organizations enforce security guardrails at the org level while delegating day-to-day access management to individual teams.

questions.title: VPC Endpoints and Network Security
questions.question: What are VPC endpoints and how do they improve security for a Spring Boot application accessing AWS services?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- VPC Endpoint: private connection to AWS services without internet/NAT Gateway
- Gateway Endpoint: S3 and DynamoDB — free, route table entry
- Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink): other services (Secrets Manager, SQS, SNS, ECR) — ENI in your VPC, costs per hour
- Security benefit: traffic stays within AWS backbone, not over internet
- Endpoint policy: restrict which resources the endpoint can access
- Cost: remove NAT Gateway charges for high-volume S3/DynamoDB traffic
- DNS: VPC endpoint overrides default DNS for the service — transparent to applications

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
By default, when a Spring Boot application running in a private subnet calls AWS services like S3, Secrets Manager, or SQS, the traffic exits through a NAT Gateway to the public internet and then back into AWS. This is a security concern — even though the traffic is encrypted, it passes over the public internet — and it's also a cost concern because NAT Gateway charges per GB of data transferred.

VPC endpoints solve both problems. A gateway endpoint for S3 and DynamoDB is a route table entry that keeps traffic within the AWS backbone — completely free and more secure. An interface endpoint for other services like Secrets Manager, SQS, or ECR creates a private network interface in your VPC. Applications connect to the service's standard DNS name, but DNS resolution returns the private IP of the endpoint — traffic never leaves the VPC.

For a production Java application, I'd always set up gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, and interface endpoints for Secrets Manager and ECR at minimum. These eliminate the NAT Gateway as a bottleneck and attack surface for those services.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Without vs With VPC Endpoint

```
Without endpoint:
ECS Task (private subnet) → NAT Gateway (public subnet) → Internet → S3
  Cost: NAT Gateway + data transfer charges
  Security: traffic over public internet (encrypted but still)

With gateway endpoint:
ECS Task (private subnet) → VPC Endpoint (route table entry) → S3
  Cost: FREE
  Security: traffic stays within AWS backbone, never touches internet
```

## Create VPC Endpoints

```bash
# Gateway endpoint for S3 (free)
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxxx \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-private-1 rtb-private-2
  # Adds route: S3 CIDR → vpce-xxxx in specified route tables

# Interface endpoint for Secrets Manager
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxxx \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.secretsmanager \
  --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
  --subnet-ids subnet-private-1 subnet-private-2 \
  --security-group-ids sg-ecs-tasks \
  --private-dns-enabled  # secretsmanager.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com resolves to private IP

# Interface endpoints you likely need:
# com.amazonaws.{region}.ecr.dkr     — pull images without NAT
# com.amazonaws.{region}.ecr.api     — ECR API calls
# com.amazonaws.{region}.secretsmanager
# com.amazonaws.{region}.ssm         — Systems Manager
# com.amazonaws.{region}.logs        — CloudWatch Logs
```

## Endpoint Policy (Restrict Access)

```json
// Endpoint policy on Secrets Manager endpoint:
// Only allow reading secrets that belong to this application
{
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-south-1:123456:secret:/prod/myapp/*"
  }]
}
// Traffic through this endpoint cannot access secrets from other applications
```

questions.title: CloudTrail and Security Monitoring
questions.question: How does AWS CloudTrail work and how do you monitor security events in a production Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- CloudTrail: logs all API calls to AWS — who did what, when, from where
- Management events: control plane — create/modify/delete resources; enabled by default
- Data events: S3 object read/write, Lambda invocation — high volume, extra cost
- Immutable audit log: store in S3 with Object Lock — prevents tampering
- CloudWatch Alarms on CloudTrail: alert on root account usage, large permission changes
- GuardDuty: ML-based threat detection — unusual API calls, crypto mining, compromised credentials
- AWS Config: continuous compliance checking — flag non-compliant resources
- Security Hub: aggregated security findings across services

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
CloudTrail records every API call made to AWS — who called it, what they called, when, from which IP, and whether it succeeded. This is the audit log for your entire AWS infrastructure. You can investigate security incidents, debug permission issues, and demonstrate compliance to auditors.

For production, store CloudTrail logs in an S3 bucket with Object Lock enabled in compliance mode. This makes logs immutable for a retention period — even administrators can't delete them. This is a compliance requirement for many security standards like SOC 2 and PCI DSS.

GuardDuty is the proactive complement to CloudTrail. It uses machine learning to analyze CloudTrail events, VPC flow logs, and DNS logs to detect anomalies — credential exfiltration, unusual API call patterns, connections to known malicious IPs, crypto mining activity. Enable it in every account and region.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## CloudTrail Setup

```bash
# Create multi-region trail (single trail covering all regions)
aws cloudtrail create-trail \
  --name org-audit-trail \
  --s3-bucket-name my-audit-logs \
  --is-multi-region-trail \
  --enable-log-file-validation  # SHA256 digest to verify log integrity

aws cloudtrail start-logging --name org-audit-trail

# S3 bucket policy: allow CloudTrail to write, deny delete
{
  "Statement": [
    {"Effect": "Allow",
     "Principal": {"Service": "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"},
     "Action": "s3:PutObject",
     "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-audit-logs/AWSLogs/*"},
    {"Effect": "Deny",
     "Principal": "*",
     "Action": ["s3:DeleteObject", "s3:DeleteObjectVersion"],
     "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-audit-logs/*"}
  ]
}
```

## CloudWatch Alarm on Security Events

```bash
# Alert when root account is used (should never happen in day-to-day ops)
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name RootAccountUsage \
  --metric-name RootAccountUsageCount \
  --namespace CloudTrailMetrics \
  --statistic Sum --period 300 --threshold 1 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:...:security-alerts

# CloudWatch Logs metric filter for root usage:
aws logs put-metric-filter \
  --log-group-name CloudTrail/Logs \
  --filter-name RootAccountUsage \
  --filter-pattern '{$.userIdentity.type="Root" && $.userIdentity.invokedBy NOT EXISTS && $.eventType !="AwsServiceEvent"}' \
  --metric-transformations 'metricName=RootAccountUsageCount,metricNamespace=CloudTrailMetrics,metricValue=1'
```

## Querying CloudTrail with Athena

```sql
-- Find all failed API calls in last 24 hours (indicates permission issues or attacks)
SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn, eventname, errormessage, sourceipaddress
FROM cloudtrail_logs
WHERE errorcode IN ('AccessDenied', 'UnauthorizedOperation')
  AND eventtime > date_format(now() - interval '1' day, '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%i:%sZ')
ORDER BY eventtime DESC
LIMIT 100;

-- Who deleted a specific S3 object?
SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn, requestparameters
FROM cloudtrail_logs
WHERE eventsource = 's3.amazonaws.com'
  AND eventname = 'DeleteObject'
  AND requestparameters LIKE '%my-important-file%';
```
